'''''Ziziphus lotus''''' is a small [[deciduous]] [[tree]] in the buckthorn [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Rhamnaceae]], native to the [[Mediterranean region]], including the [[Sahara]] in [[Morocco]] and also [[Somalia]]. It is one of several species called "'''jujube'''", and is closely related to ''[[Ziziphus jujuba|Z. jujuba]]'', the true jujube.

==Description==
''Ziziphus lotus'' can reach a height of {{convert|2|-|5|m|ft}}, with shiny green leaves about 5 cm long. The edible fruit is a globose, dark yellow [[drupe]] of 1–1.5 cm diameter.{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}}

==Cultural and religious references==
''Ziziphus lotus'' is often regarded as the [[lotus tree]] of [[Greek mythology]].<ref name=Herodotus>Herodotus, ''[[Histories (Herodotus)|Histories]]'', Book IV, 177.</ref> It is thought to be referenced in the ''[[Odyssey]]'', consumed by the Lotus-Eaters as a [[narcotic]] to induce peaceful [[apathy]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Truesdale |first=Jack |date=22 July 2026 |title=What Were the Lotus-Eaters Eating in Homer's 'Odyssey'? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/22/science/odyssey-lotus-eaters-opium.html |access-date=24 July 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

A sacred lotus tree planted near the [[temple of Vulcan]] in Rome was said to have been planted by [[Romulus]], who is said to have been a contemporary of the composer[s] of the ''Odyssey'' (8th century BCE); it was still standing some 700 years later, in the time of [[Pliny the Elder]].<ref>{{Cite DGRBM|article=Vulcanus}}</ref>

In Arabic-speaking regions, ''Ziziphus lotus'', and alternatively ''[[Jujube|Ziziphus jujuba]]'', are closely associated with the [[Sidrat al-Muntaha|lote-trees]] (''sidr'') which are mentioned in the [[Quran]],<ref>[[Abdullah Yusuf Ali|Abdullah, Yusuf Ali]] (1946) ''The Holy Qur-an. Text, Translation and Commentary'', Qatar National Printing Press, p. 1139, n. 3814</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Sidrah (Lote-Tree) and the Sidrat al-Muntaha (Lote-Tree of the Extremity): Some Apects of their Islamic and Bābī-Bahā'ī {{sic|nolink=y|reason=error in source|Intepretations}}. |author=Stephen Lambden |quote=This is apparently the wild jujube or zizyphus spina-christi  (Christ's thorn), a tall, stout, tropical tree (see image above) with dense prickly branches which produces a sweet reddish fruit similar to that of the jujube (the `unnāb = zizyphus vulgaris / fruit) |url=https://hurqalya.ucmerced.edu/node/38 |access-date=9 July 2019 |archive-date=9 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190709132946/https://hurqalya.ucmerced.edu/node/38 |url-status=live }}</ref> while in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]], it is rather ''[[Ziziphus spina-christi]]'' that is called ''sidr''.<ref>{{cite book |title=Illustrated Bible Dictionary and Treasury of Biblical History, Biography, Geography, Doctrine, and Literature |author-link=Matthew George Easton|last=Easton|first=M.G.|year=1893 |location=London, Edinburgh and New York |publisher=T. Nelson and Sons |page=688 }}</ref> Elsewhere in the Arab world, the European and [[Jujube|Chinese jujubes]] are also associated with the lote-trees (''sidr'').<ref>[[Abdullah Yusuf Ali|Abdullah, Yusuf Ali]] (1946) ''The Holy Qur-an. Text, Translation and Commentary'', Qatar National Printing Press.p.1139, n.3814</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Sidrah (Lote-Tree) and the Sidrat al-Muntaha (Lote-Tree of the Extremity): Some Aspects of their Islamic and Bābī-Bahā'ī {{sic|nolink=y|reason=error in source|Intepretations}}. |author=Stephen Lambden |quote=This is apparently the wild jujube or ''Zizyphus spina-christi'' (Christ's thorn), a tall, stout, tropical tree (see image above) with dense prickly branches which produces a sweet reddish fruit similar to that of the jujube (the `unnāb = ''Zizyphus vulgaris'' / fruit) |url=https://hurqalya.ucmerced.edu/node/38 |access-date=9 July 2019 |archive-date=9 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190709132946/https://hurqalya.ucmerced.edu/node/38 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The 19th century English explorer [[Richard Francis Burton|Richard Burton]] reported seeing an ancient ''sidr'' tree in the mosque containing the [[Al-Masjid an-Nabawi|Prophet Muhammad's tomb]] in [[Medina]]. It was in a garden dedicated to the prophet's daughter, [[Fatima]]. The fruit from the tree was being sold to pilgrims and its leaves used for washing dead bodies.<ref>[[Richard Francis Burton|Burton, Sir Richard Francis]] (1855) ''A Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to Al-Madinah and Meccah''  p. 337</ref>
